title: How Our Tiny Karting Team Made It to Nationals
creator: Liam Doherty
description:
The story of three kids, one secondhand kart, and a very patient dad. 2009 to 2013.

Photos and old camcorder footage courtesy of my mum, who kept absolutely everything.

If you raced at Mondello or Watergrasshill back then, say hi in the comments.

sentences.t: So this is a story I've wanted to tell on the channel for ages.
When I was twelve, my brother, my cousin and I decided we were going to be racing drivers.
We had no money, no experience, and absolutely no idea what we were doing.
Four years later, we were on the grid at the national championship.
It started with a kart my dad found on a buy and sell website for four hundred euro.
It was ancient, the chassis was bent, and the engine smoked like a chimney.
We spent the whole winter in my granny's garage taking it apart and putting it back together, mostly wrong.
Our first race was at a little track outside Cork, and I finished dead last by almost a full lap.
I was devastated, but my dad just said, right, so we know where we're starting from.
The thing nobody tells you about karting is how expensive it gets, really fast.
Tyres, fuel, entry fees, ferry tickets once we started racing in the UK.
By the second season, we were burning through money my parents genuinely didn't have.
So my dad did something I still can't believe he did.
He put on his one good suit and went door to door around our town asking local businesses to be our sponsors.
Most of them said no, obviously, it was the middle of a recession.
But Doyle's Motors, the garage at the end of our road, said yes and paid for our tyres for the whole season.
The chipper on Main Street sponsored us too, and in return they got their logo on the nose cone, which, to be fair, was a terrible logo.
We had the stickers made at a print shop and I remember putting them on the kart like it was a Formula One car.
Every Monday after a race, my brother and I would go into Doyle's and tell old Mick how we'd done, and he'd pin the results up behind the counter.
Having people in town who cared how we did changed everything.
We started taking it seriously.
We'd walk every track before the race, learning the braking points, figuring out where the grip was.
My cousin turned out to be the best mechanic of the three of us, so he stopped driving and ran the setup instead.
And slowly, we started finishing races in the middle of the pack, and then near the front.
In 2012, my brother won his first race in the wet at Mondello.
Everyone else was on slicks, and my cousin made the call to switch to wets five minutes before the start.
He won by eleven seconds, which in karting is an eternity.
I think my dad cried, though he still denies it.
And that result got us enough points to qualify for the nationals the next summer.
The nationals themselves were, honestly, a bit of a reality check.
Some of the teams there had full-time mechanics, brand new chassis and a truck with an awning.
We had a borrowed trailer and a gazebo that blew away on the first morning.
I qualified twenty-second out of thirty-four and finished nineteenth in the final.
My brother had an engine failure on lap six, and he sat on the tyre wall for the rest of the race with his helmet still on.
None of us went on to race professionally.
My brother's an engineer now, my cousin runs his own garage, and I make videos on the internet.
But that old kart is still in my granny's garage, with the chipper's terrible logo still on the front.
Next week I'm going to try and get it running again, so subscribe if you want to see that disaster.
Thanks for watching.
